name: Vitamin C, scurvy & the Royal Navy
strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
scope: The hook: a disease that rotted sailors' gums and reopened old wounds on long voyages, cured by ordinary fresh fruit. T1: scurvy strikes when there's no fresh food for months (bleeding gums, loose teeth, wounds that won't heal); the fix is fresh CITRUS (oranges & lemons). T2: the missing thing is vitamin C, needed to build COLLAGEN, the 'glue' holding skin, gums and blood vessels together, so without it the body literally comes apart. T2 (surprise source): a raw red BELL PEPPER carries more vitamin C than an orange (also broccoli, blackcurrants) — citrus isn't the only star. T3: James Lind's 1747 trial aboard HMS Salisbury gave sailors different remedies; only the pair on oranges & lemons recovered — one of the first controlled clinical experiments. T3: the word 'ascorbic acid' literally means 'anti-scurvy' (a-scorbutic). T3: the Navy issued citrus juice from ~1795, earning British sailors the nickname 'limeys.' T4: the Navy later swapped Mediterranean LEMONS for cheaper West Indian LIMES — but limes hold far LESS vitamin C, and boiling the juice and storing it in copper destroyed most of what remained, so scurvy came BACK on polar expeditions. T4: humans (and guinea pigs) are among the rare animals that CAN'T make their own vitamin C — a broken GULO gene — so we must eat it, while a dog's liver makes its own. T5: vitamin C is fragile, wrecked by heat, air, light and time (why long-stored juice failed). T5 (payoff): shelf-stable vitamin C came from FERMENTED food — Captain Cook carried sauerkraut (fermented cabbage keeps its C) to keep crews scurvy-free.
source: Grokipedia/page/Scurvy attempted FIRST but returned HTTP 403 to the fetcher; corroborated via en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scurvy (fetched: Lind 1747 HMS Salisbury controlled trial; 1795 Admiralty lemon ration; Napoleonic-era switch to West Indian limes with lower vitamin C, degraded by light/air/copper tubing; 1918 study found Navy lime juice near-zero antiscorbutic power → polar-expedition scurvy; 'limey' origin; GULO pseudogene). Bell-pepper vitamin C content and sauerkraut/Cook: standard nutrition + maritime-history consensus (build stage to pull primary cite).
framing_note: Scene-led (a sailor's mouth falling apart), never 'What is vitamin C?'; every answer is a concrete food/history fact. KEY RAIL: the lime switch BACKFIRED — limes had LESS vitamin C than lemons, do not imply lime was an upgrade; and don't anachronistically credit Lind with 'vitamin C' (isolated only in the 1930s) — he knew citrus worked, not why. Dinner-test payoff = the sauerkraut rung (fermented cabbage as the shelf-stable cure).

name: Vitamin A: liver, orange veg & the carrot myth
strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
scope: The hook: the propaganda story that carrots give you night vision, and the food that really is a vitamin-A bomb. T1: vitamin A powers dim-light sight (real deficiency causes night blindness) and the single richest food source is LIVER — a small piece packs a huge dose. T2: orange and dark-green veg (carrots, sweet potato, pumpkin, spinach, kale) supply it as BETA-CAROTENE, the orange pigment the body converts to vitamin A. T2: egg yolks, butter and whole milk carry ready-made vitamin A (retinol) — the fat is why. T3: the 'carrots for super night vision' claim is HALF-true — fixing a deficiency restores normal night sight, but extra carrots past adequacy give no superpower. T3 (history): the myth was WWII British propaganda — the RAF credited ace John 'Cat's Eyes' Cunningham's carrot habit for his night kills to HIDE that pilots were using secret airborne radar. T4: plant beta-carotene is self-limiting (the body converts only what it needs, so you can't poison yourself — though enough turns skin orange, carotenemia); animal retinol is NOT capped. T4: because retinol isn't capped, some animal liver is TOO rich — polar-bear and seal liver hold such concentrated vitamin A that eating them poisons a person (headache, peeling skin). T5 (payoff): in 1913 Antarctic explorers Mawson and Mertz, starving, ate their sled DOGS' livers — vitamin A poisoning killed Mertz (skin peeling off); the Inuit had always known never to eat polar-bear liver. T5: vitamin A is fat-soluble, so cooking carrots in butter/oil unlocks far more of the carotene than eating them dry.
source: Carrot myth / John 'Cat's Eyes' Cunningham / AI radar cover story: Smithsonian Magazine, CEENTA, Atlas Obscura, Explore the Archive (all consulted). Liver toxicity / Mawson & Mertz 1913 Far Eastern Party / Inuit avoidance / de Veer 1597 / husky-liver toxic dose: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypervitaminosis_A and A-Z Animals (consulted). Beta-carotene conversion + self-limiting + fat-soluble absorption: standard nutrition consensus.
framing_note: Invert the wonder — put the propaganda claim / the 'liver that kills' in the stem, make the knowable food-fact the answer; never a definition. KEY RAIL: the carrot claim is HALF-true (restores normal night vision in deficiency, no super-vision) — don't over-debunk into 'carrots do nothing for eyes,' and only ANIMAL retinol overdoses, never plant beta-carotene. Dinner-test payoff = the Mawson/Mertz sled-dog-liver rung.

name: Niacin, pellagra & why corn must be nixtamalized
strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
scope: The hook: a people living on corn get a disease of the skin and the mind — and an ancient soaking trick was the cure all along. T1: a near corn-only diet brings PELLAGRA, the 'four D's' — dermatitis (sun-scorched skin), diarrhea, dementia, death. T2: the missing nutrient is niacin (vitamin B3); corn actually HAS niacin but locked in a form the body can't unlock, and corn is low in tryptophan (which the body can turn into niacin). T3: Mesoamericans solved it thousands of years ago by NIXTAMALIZATION — soaking dried corn in alkaline limewater or wood-ash water before grinding. T3: the alkali releases the bound niacin AND turns the corn into masa, the dough for tortillas and tamales — so those cultures ate corn for millennia with no pellagra. T4: when corn spread to Europe and the American South WITHOUT the soaking step (they took the crop, not the technique), pellagra epidemics exploded across the early-1900s US South. T4: Dr. Joseph Goldberger proved pellagra was DIETARY, not a germ — he showed adding meat, milk and eggs cured it. T5 (payoff): the true villain was a monotonous poverty diet, not corn itself — niacin-rich meat, milk, eggs and fish prevent pellagra, and the indigenous soaking wisdom beat the 'modern' corn-only diet. T5: that same alkaline treatment is what gives a corn tortilla and tortilla chips their distinctive flavor.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pellagra and /Nixtamalization (consulted: bound niacin/niacytin, low tryptophan, calcium-hydroxide limewater NOT the fruit, tryptophan→niacin, US South epidemic, Goldberger). Southern Foodways Alliance 'Malnourished' + New World Encyclopedia Pellagra (Goldberger, spring sickness, indigenous immunity). Corroborates strongly across sources.
framing_note: Scene-led (the corn-eating village falling ill / the ancient soaking pot), never 'What is niacin?'; the answer is always a food or food-history fact. CRITICAL RAIL: the 'lime' in limewater is CALCIUM HYDROXIDE (alkali), NOT the citrus fruit — a build must never confuse them; nixtamalization is pre-Columbian Mesoamerican; pellagra is a DEFICIENCY, not a contagion (Goldberger's whole point). Dinner-test payoff = Goldberger proving diet-not-germ / traditional wisdom beat the modern mono-diet.

name: Iron: heme (meat) vs non-heme (plants)
strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
scope: The hook: two foods list the same iron on the label, but your body pulls far more from one. T1: iron lets red blood cells carry oxygen; run low and you get anemia (tired, pale, cold); red meat is the classic iron food. T2: there are two kinds — HEME iron (from meat and blood, the animal kind) which the body absorbs easily, and NON-HEME iron (from beans, lentils, spinach) which it absorbs poorly. T3: vitamin C dramatically boosts the weak plant iron — squeeze lemon on the lentils, eat peppers with the beans. T3: tannins in tea and coffee, and phytates in whole grains, BLOCK iron — a cup of tea with dinner cuts how much you absorb. T4: spinach's iron-powerhouse reputation is overrated — it has iron but oxalates bind it, so little gets in (Popeye is legend, not nutrition). T4: cooking acidic food like tomato sauce in a CAST-IRON pan leaches real, usable (non-heme) iron into the food. T5 (payoff): this is the honest core of 'why a kid needs some red meat' — heme iron from meat is the one reliably well-absorbed source, which is why iron-deficiency is more common in those who eat none, and why plant-iron eaters must lean on the vitamin-C trick.
source: PubMed 11124756 (ascorbic acid enhances non-heme iron absorption; ~67% boost at 100mg vitamin C in single meals). Cast-iron leaching (~up to 16%, acidic/moist/long-cooked foods, non-heme form): appetise.io and WhatsCookingAmerica (consulted). Heme vs non-heme absorption ranges + tannin/phytate inhibition + spinach oxalate: standard nutrition consensus.
framing_note: Scene-led (two dinners, one gives you the iron) and food-anchored; invert with the label-vs-absorption puzzle. RAIL: spinach iron is poorly absorbed (Popeye = legend); cast iron adds the NON-heme form. Steel-man both sides — plant-iron diets work WITH vitamin C pairing, don't strawman vegetarians — but state the honest asymmetry (heme absorbs best). Dinner-test payoff = the heme-iron 'why red meat' rung. vision_mandated because the payoff makes the bank's traditional-foods dietary claim.

name: Fat-soluble vitamins need fat (eat the butter with the veg)
strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
scope: The hook: you can eat the vitamin and still not absorb a bit of it. T1: some vitamins dissolve in water (C and the B's), and four dissolve only in FAT — the fat-soluble crew is A, D, E, K. T2: because they ride in fat, a fat-FREE meal wastes them — a dry salad of carrots and greens with zero fat lets much of the vitamin A pass straight through. T3: the fix is delicious — add oil, butter, cheese, avocado or a little meat and absorption jumps; olive-oil dressing isn't just flavor, it unlocks the nutrients. T3: mechanism — dietary fat triggers bile, which packages the vitamins into tiny droplets (micelles) the gut wall can take up; no fat, no carrier. T4: this is a real strike against the fat-free fad — skim milk and fat-free dressing can strand the fat-soluble vitamins, while whole milk and full-fat dressing absorb better. T4: unlike water-soluble vitamins (excess peed out daily), fat-soluble ones are STORED in the liver and body fat — you don't need them every day, but you CAN overdose (the polar-bear-liver vitamin A). T5 (payoff): the old-fashioned pairing was right — butter on the vegetables, oil on the salad, cheese with the broccoli; 'eat the butter with the veg' is smart nutrition, not a guilty indulgence.
source: NCBI Bookshelf NBK234920 (Fat-Soluble Vitamins, RDA — micelle/bile absorption, storage) and PMC11242131 (A/D/E/K clinical review) consulted. ScienceDirect randomized crossover trial on dietary fat & carotenoid absorption (consulted: adding fat raises carotenoid uptake; absorption drops sharply below ~5g fat/meal). Water- vs fat-soluble storage/excretion: standard consensus.
framing_note: Scene-led (the dry salad that wastes its own vitamins), food-anchored answers only. RAIL: the mnemonic is A/D/E/K; fat-soluble are STORED and can build up (contrast water-soluble excreted). LEAN (steel-man both): the absorption mechanism is settled science, but the payoff pushes against low-fat orthodoxy toward whole/traditional fats — present the low-fat side fairly, then the pairing case. Dinner-test payoff = the 'eat the butter with the veg' rung. vision_mandated for the fat-orthodoxy lean.

name: Vitamin D: sunlight, fatty fish & the rickets story
strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
scope: The hook: the one vitamin your own skin manufactures — and the disease that appeared when cities blocked the sun. T1: vitamin D is the 'sunshine vitamin' — your SKIN makes it when sunlight hits it, the one vitamin you don't strictly need from food. T2: in food the best sources are fatty fish (salmon, mackerel, sardines) plus egg yolks; it's rare enough that milk is often fortified with it. T2: the old remedy was cod liver oil — a spoonful of fish-liver oil loaded with vitamin D (and A). T3: too little in childhood causes RICKETS — soft bones that bow under a child's weight into bowed legs, because calcium can't harden bone without vitamin D. T3 (history): rickets exploded in the smoky, sunless industrial cities of 1800s Britain — tall tenements and coal smog kept sunlight off slum children. T4: the skin makes vitamin D from UVB sunlight acting on a cholesterol-like molecule, so darker skin (more melanin) needs more sun and far-north winters make food sources matter more. T4 (payoff): traditional far-north diets beat the no-sun problem with food — the Inuit got vitamin D from fatty fish and marine-mammal fat, not sunlight.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_D and NCBI Endotext NBK278935 (7-dehydrocholesterol + UVB 290-320nm synthesis; fatty fish/fish-liver-oil sources). PubMed 30627846 (cod liver oil, UV radiation, eradication of rickets). Rickets in industrial cities + melanin/latitude: consensus across the consulted sources.
framing_note: Scene-led (the sunless slum child, the spoon of cod liver oil), answers are foods or the disease. RAIL: skin makes it from UVB SUNLIGHT specifically (not warmth or visible light); rickets is the childhood bone-softening disease. Mostly settled science (optimal-dose debate exists but core is not contested) so vision_mandated:false. Dinner-test payoff = the Inuit fatty-fish/marine-fat rung (food replacing the missing sun).

name: B12: the animal-only vitamin & why vegans supplement
strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
scope: The hook: the one nutrient a whole-foods plant diet simply cannot supply. T1: vitamin B12 keeps nerves and red blood cells healthy, and it lives in meat, fish, eggs and dairy — essentially NOT in plant foods. T2: the richest sources by far are liver and shellfish (clams). T3: the twist — B12 isn't made by animals OR plants, it's made by BACTERIA; animals bank it from microbes, which is why it ends up only in animal tissue. T3: that's why strict vegans must take a B12 supplement or fortified foods — a plants-only diet has no reliable source, and deficiency creeps in over years because the liver stores a big reserve. T4: even with plenty in the diet some people can't absorb it — the stomach must make 'intrinsic factor' to ferry B12 across the gut; without it you get pernicious anemia. T4 (payoff): the honest steel-man — a well-planned vegan diet CAN be healthy IF B12 is supplemented, but B12 is the clearest case where a plants-only diet cannot be sourced from whole foods alone.
source: Britannica 'vitamin B12' (bacterial synthesis; liver/viscera richest; vegans risk deficiency without supplements/fortified foods). NCBI StatPearls NBK441923 (intrinsic factor, pernicious anemia, ~3-year vegan-diet deficiency onset). Corroborated across both.
framing_note: Scene-led (the strict-vegan plate missing one thing), food-anchored answers. RAIL: B12 is made by BACTERIA, not synthesized by the animal itself; deficiency is slow because of liver stores. STANCE — steel-man both sides genuinely: supplemented vegan diets work fine, do NOT strawman vegans, but state honestly that B12 is the non-negotiable animal-food gap. Dinner-test payoff = the T4 steel-man rung. vision_mandated because it engages the vegan-diet debate.

name: Calcium: dairy, greens & why spinach lies
strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
scope: The hook: two greens list the same calcium, but one hands almost none over. T1: calcium builds bones and teeth and fires muscles; the classic source is dairy — milk, cheese, yogurt. T2: plants supply it too — leafy greens like kale, collards, bok choy and broccoli. T3: but greens aren't equal — spinach LOOKS calcium-rich yet its oxalates lock most of it up, so you absorb far more from kale or collards than from the same spinach. T3: a sneaky top source is canned sardines and salmon — the tiny soft bones (softened by canning) are almost pure calcium, eaten without noticing. T4: calcium needs vitamin D to be absorbed at all — the link between the 'sunshine vitamin' and strong bones, and why they're paired in fortified milk. T4 (payoff): the smartest calcium foods carry their own helpers — canned sardines deliver calcium PLUS vitamin D PLUS fat in one bite, an all-in-one bone package.
source: PMC8746734 (calcium bioavailability / food-matrix effects; spinach ~5% absorbed due to oxalate vs low-oxalate greens). AlgaeCal & Kaplan Clinic (spinach oxalate binding; kale/collards higher usable calcium). Hancock Health (non-dairy sources; canned sardine/salmon soft-bone calcium). Consistent across sources.
framing_note: Scene-led (the spinach that looks like a calcium hero and isn't), food-anchored answers. RAIL: spinach calcium is bound by OXALATE so poorly absorbed — kale/collards win; calcium needs vitamin D to be absorbed. Settled science → vision_mandated:false. Dinner-test payoff = the canned-sardine-bones rung (the all-in-one calcium+D+fat package).

name: Thiamine & beriberi: how polishing rice white made people sick
strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
scope: The hook: making rice prettier and whiter set off an epidemic. T1: when Asian diets switched to polished WHITE rice, a crippling disease spread — beriberi (nerve damage, weakness, swelling, heart failure). T2: the missing nutrient is thiamine (vitamin B1), which lives in the rice's bran and germ — the exact outer layers polishing scrapes off to make rice white. T3: Christiaan Eijkman noticed hospital chickens fed leftover polished rice developed a beriberi-like paralysis and recovered when the bran was put back — an accidental clue that a MISSING food factor, not a germ, caused disease. T3: in the Japanese Navy, Kanehiro Takaki slashed beriberi by replacing white-rice rations with barley, meat, fish and vegetables — a diet fix decades before anyone knew what a vitamin was. T4 (payoff): beriberi, alongside scurvy and pellagra, helped BIRTH the very idea of a 'vitamin' — that food holds tiny essential factors whose ABSENCE causes disease. T4: the lesson still holds — over-refining a whole grain strips nutrients, and brown rice keeps the thiamine that white rice throws away.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thiamine_deficiency and /Takaki_Kanehiro (consulted). The Hospitalist 'History of a Vitamin' and Atlas Obscura 'How Killer Rice Crippled Tokyo and the Japanese Navy' (Eijkman's chickens 1897; Takaki's Navy diet reform eliminating beriberi within years; bran contains thiamine). Corroborated.
framing_note: Scene-led (the whiter rice that sickened a navy), answers are food/food-history facts. RAIL: thiamine sits in the BRAN/GERM removed by polishing; Eijkman's chicken finding was an accidental clue and Takaki fixed it by diet BEFORE the 'vitamin' concept existed — don't credit them with knowing the molecule. Lightly supports the anti-over-refined lean but is settled history → vision_mandated:false. Dinner-test payoff = the T4 'birth of the vitamin idea' rung.

name: Iodine: iodized salt & the end of the goiter belt
strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
scope: The hook: a swollen neck that vanished when they changed one thing in the salt shaker. T1: the thyroid gland needs iodine to work; without it the thyroid swells into a big neck lump — a goiter. T2: iodine comes from the SEA — fish, shellfish and especially seaweed are loaded, while people far inland often fell short. T3: whole inland regions were 'goiter belts' — the US Great Lakes/Midwest and the Swiss Alps had iodine-poor soil; in 1920s Michigan, 70-100% of schoolchildren in some areas had goiters. T3: the fix (1924, Michigan) was brilliantly cheap — add a trace of iodine to ordinary table SALT, since everyone already eats salt. T4 (payoff): it did more than shrink goiters — iodine deficiency in pregnancy stunts a child's brain, so iodized salt quietly RAISED average intelligence in the deficient regions. T4: severe deficiency in infancy caused cretinism (stunted growth and mental disability) — a great preventable harm erased by the right pinch of salt.
source: Healio 'Iodized salt: centennial' and Michigan Public 'goiter belt' (consulted: iodine-poor upper-Midwest soil; 1920s 70-100% schoolchild goiter rates; 1924 Michigan iodized salt, Morton national rollout; Michigan goiter ~30%→<2% in a decade). PMC6919660 (cognitive effects of US salt iodization). Washington Post 100-years piece. Corroborated.
framing_note: Scene-led (the neck lump / the schoolroom full of goiters), food-anchored answers (salt, seafood, seaweed). RAIL: iodine comes from the SEA (inland soil is poor); the intervention is iodized TABLE SALT, 1924 Michigan; deficiency in pregnancy/infancy harms the brain (cretinism). Settled → vision_mandated:false. Dinner-test payoff = the T4 rung (iodized salt raised children's intelligence).

name: Folate: the leaf vitamin
strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
scope: The hook: a vitamin literally named after leaves. T1: folate (vitamin B9) takes its name from the Latin folium, 'leaf,' because it was first pulled from leafy greens like spinach. T2: the best food sources are dark leafy greens, legumes (beans, lentils) and — again — liver. T3: folate is vital in early pregnancy — too little causes neural-tube defects like spina bifida, where the baby's spine doesn't close properly. T3: because that happens in the first weeks, often before a woman knows she's pregnant, many countries add folic acid to flour and bread by law, and birth defects dropped sharply. T4 (payoff): heat and water are folate's enemies — boiling greens leaches and destroys much of it, so raw or lightly-steamed greens keep more; the leaf vitamin is a fragile one.
source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Folate and Fill Your Plate 'The Discovery of the Vitamin Folate' (consulted: folium='leaf', first isolated from spinach 1941 by Mitchell/Snell/Williams; Lucy Wills 1931 pregnancy anemia). Codeage folate history + NTD fortification data. Corroborated.
framing_note: Invert the wonder — put the 'named after a plant part' hook in the stem, answer is the leaf/food fact; never 'What is folate?'. RAIL: folium = 'leaf'; neural-tube defects form in the first weeks (why folate matters BEFORE and at conception, not just during). Settled → vision_mandated:false. Dinner-test payoff = the T4 fragility rung (boiling destroys folate, eat greens raw/steamed).

name: What cooking does to vitamins: why steaming beats boiling
strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
scope: The hook: the vitamins you pour down the drain. T1: cooking can DESTROY vitamins — vitamin C is the fragile one, wrecked by heat and dissolved out into the cooking water. T2: that's why STEAMING or microwaving vegetables keeps more vitamins than BOILING — the veg never soaks in water that carries the vitamins away. T3: the split — WATER-soluble vitamins (C and the B's) leach into cooking water and break down with heat; FAT-soluble ones (A, D, E, K) shrug off heat but can be lost in fat you drain off. T3: the pro move is to keep the vitamin-rich cooking water for soup, gravy or stock (the traditional 'pot liquor') so the leached vitamins aren't wasted. T4 (payoff): cooking isn't all loss — heat breaks down cell walls to RELEASE nutrients raw food locks away: cooked tomatoes yield more usable lycopene, cooked carrots more usable beta-carotene than raw.
source: Water- vs fat-soluble heat/leaching behavior: NCBI NBK234920 and PMC11242131 (fat-soluble stability) plus standard food-science consensus. Heat-released lycopene (cooked tomato) and beta-carotene bioavailability: well-established food-science consensus (Cornell/Rui Hai Liu tomato-lycopene work; USDA retention data) — build stage to attach primary cites; not fabricated but not re-verified live this session.
framing_note: Scene-led (the pot of boiling water stealing the vitamins) and prep-framed (the game action is cooking — 'you steam it / you boil it' voice is fine). RAIL: water-soluble (C, B) leach + degrade with heat; fat-soluble (A,D,E,K) survive heat; and cooking is NOT pure loss — some nutrients (lycopene, beta-carotene) rise with heat. Settled → vision_mandated:false. Dinner-test payoff = the T4 rung (cooking can INCREASE available nutrients).

name: Variety beats any single superfood
strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
scope: The hook: every 'miracle food' is missing something. T2: no single food is complete — the body needs dozens of different nutrients that no one ingredient supplies, so any lone 'superfood' leaves a gap. T3: the proof is written in disease — scurvy, beriberi, pellagra and goiter were every one a disease of MONOTONY (citrus-less voyages, white rice, corn-only, no seafood); variety is the oldest cure. T3: 'eat the rainbow' is real nutrition, not a slogan — different colors are different protective compounds: orange = carotene, red tomato = lycopene, purple = anthocyanins, deep green = folate and vitamin K. T4 (payoff): the honest steel-man — 'superfoods' like blueberries and kale genuinely are nutritious; the error is the MARKETING that sells one food (or one pill) as a shortcut. Whole-food variety, not a hero ingredient, is what actually works.
source: Synthesizes the verified deficiency-disease ladders in this sub-strand (scurvy=vitamin C, beriberi=thiamine, pellagra=niacin, goiter=iodine — each corroborated above). 'Eat the rainbow' phytonutrient color→compound mapping (carotene/lycopene/anthocyanin) and superfood-marketing critique: standard nutrition consensus.
framing_note: Scene-led (the marketed 'miracle food' that can't stand alone), food-anchored answers (name the color's compound, name the monotony disease). RAIL: do NOT strawman — superfoods ARE nutritious; the target is the SHORTCUT claim, not the food. LEAN (steel-man both): mainstream 'balanced diet' and the traditional whole-food-variety view converge here against reductionist single-food/pill marketing. vision_mandated:true (nutrition-stance topic). Dinner-test payoff = the T4 superfood steel-man rung.

name: Vitamin K & the fermented-food payoff
strand: Micros: vitamins & where you get them
scope: The hook: why this vitamin got the letter K, out of alphabetical order. T3: vitamin K is the CLOTTING vitamin — its job is to make blood clot and seal wounds; the 'K' comes from the Danish word Koagulation, named by its discoverer Henrik Dam. T3: the everyday form (K1) comes from leafy greens — kale, spinach, broccoli — the green leaves again. T4 (payoff): a second form, K2, comes from FERMENTED and animal foods — aged cheese, egg yolk, and above all natto, the sticky fermented soybeans of Japan (made by Bacillus subtilis bacteria). T4: K2's emerging role is as a 'traffic cop' for calcium, steering it into bones and teeth and away from clogging arteries — a reason traditional fermented and grass-fed foods are prized.
source: Vitamin K discovery (Henrik Dam, Danish 'koagulation', 1929/1935, 1943 Nobel), K1 phylloquinone in leafy greens, K2 menaquinone in natto/cheese/organ meat (MK-7 from Bacillus subtilis natto): consulted search across dsm-firmenich, boltpharmacy, Oxford Vitality, en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vitamin_K. K2→arterial-calcium role: EMERGING science (Rotterdam Study lineage) — flag as emerging, not settled.
framing_note: Invert the wonder — the stem asks why it's 'K' (out of order); answer is the koagulation/clotting fact; never a definition-shell. RAIL: K = koagulation (Danish, Dam); K1 = greens, K2 = fermented/animal; the K2-steers-calcium-from-arteries claim is EMERGING, present it as promising-not-proven. vision_mandated:true (the K2/arterial-calcium traditional-foods claim is contested/emerging). Dinner-test payoff = the natto/fermented-food K2 rung.
